properties.name: Hadrian acclaimed emperor at Antioch
properties.image_credit: Roman marble copy of Eutychides' Tyche of Antioch, Vatican Museums · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Marble statue personifying the city of Antioch, crowned with a mural crown
properties.one_line: The legions at Antioch proclaimed Hadrian emperor on 11 August, the exact day this map is set — news of Trajan's death two days earlier having just reached the city.

properties.name: Kitos War — Cyrenaica revolt
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Cyrene, Libya · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Jewish rebels under Lukuas devastated Cyrenaica so thoroughly that Hadrian later had to send fresh colonists to resettle the depopulated province.

properties.name: Kitos War — Egypt suppression
properties.image_credit: O. Von Corven, 19th-century engraving imagining ancient Alexandria's public buildings · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century engraving imagining the grand public buildings of ancient Alexandria
properties.one_line: Marcius Turbo's combined land and naval force retook Alexandria from Lukuas's rebels and pacified the Egyptian countryside by autumn 117.

properties.name: Kitos War — Cyprus revolt at Salamis
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Salamis, Cyprus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological ruins at ancient Salamis, Cyprus
properties.one_line: Jewish rebels under Artemion razed Salamis, the provincial capital of Cyprus, prompting Rome to ban Jews from the island afterward, even shipwreck survivors.

properties.name: Kitos War — Mesopotamia and Babylonia revolt
properties.image_credit: 1864 photograph of the ancient ruins near Ctesiphon · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
properties.one_line: Jewish communities across newly-conquered Mesopotamia rose against Rome in the rear of Trajan's Parthian campaign, and were suppressed by Lusius Quietus before he moved on to Judaea.

properties.name: Siege of Lydda
properties.image_credit: The Lod Mosaic, a Roman-period floor mosaic found at Lod (ancient Lydda) — a later find from the same town, photo by Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Lusius Quietus besieged the Judaean town of Lydda, where rebels had gathered under Julianus and Pappus and Rabban Gamaliel II was trapped inside.

properties.name: Execution of the Martyrs of Lydda
properties.image_credit: The Lod Mosaic, a Roman-period floor mosaic found at Lod (ancient Lydda) — a later find from the same town, photo by Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Rebel leaders Julianus and Pappus were captured and executed at Lydda, remembered afterward in rabbinic sources as the "slain of Lydda."

properties.name: Trajan captures Ctesiphon
properties.image_credit: 1864 photograph of the ancient ruins near Ctesiphon · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
properties.one_line: Trajan took the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in 116, briefly installing a puppet king and forming the short-lived province of Mesopotamia.

properties.name: Parthian War — Roman position collapses
properties.one_line: By 117 the failed siege of Hatra and renewed Parthian resistance had unraveled Trajan's conquests, and Rome's brief hold on Mesopotamia was already being abandoned as the emperor withdrew toward Syria.

properties.name: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa founded
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: The new provincial capital of Dacia, built from scratch after the 106 conquest and named for Trajan, was by 117 a going colonia with forum, amphitheater, and governor's palace.

properties.name: Gold rush at Alburnus Maior
properties.image_credit: Roman gallery at the Rosia Montana gold mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)
properties.one_line: Illyrian colonists worked Rome's new Dacian gold mines at Alburnus Maior, the wealth that had driven Trajan's two Dacian wars in the first place.

properties.name: Petra under Roman rule
properties.image_credit: Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), Petra · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Rock-cut facade of Al-Khazneh at Petra, carved into pink sandstone cliffs
properties.one_line: The former Nabataean royal capital lost its political status when Trajan annexed the kingdom in 106, though it remained the province's religious center.

properties.name: Bostra made capital of Arabia Petraea
properties.one_line: Trajan made Bostra the new capital and legionary base of the province of Arabia Petraea after annexing the Nabataean kingdom in 106.

properties.name: Trajan's Column dedicated
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Column, Rome, dedicated 113 CE · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: The 30-meter marble column narrating the Dacian Wars in a spiraling relief was dedicated in Trajan's new forum on 12 May 113.

properties.name: Forum and Markets of Trajan dedicated
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Market, Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Apollodorus of Damascus's vast new forum complex, funded by the spoils of the Dacian Wars, was dedicated in January 112 alongside its adjoining market halls.

properties.name: Aqua Traiana opened
properties.one_line: Trajan's new aqueduct began delivering spring water from Lake Bracciano, 57 kilometers away, into the Trastevere district and the Janiculum in 109.

properties.name: Antioch earthquake
properties.image_credit: Roman-era mosaic excavated at Antioch · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: A massive earthquake leveled much of Antioch while Trajan was wintering there for the Parthian campaign, killing the consul Marcus Pedo Vergilianus and nearly the emperor himself.

properties.name: Trajan dies at Selinus
properties.one_line: The 63-year-old emperor died at Selinus in western Cilicia on 8 August 117, worn out and gravely ill weeks after abandoning his failed siege of Hatra; the town was afterward renamed Trajanopolis in his memory.

properties.name: Trajan's adoption letter reaches Hadrian
properties.one_line: A letter announcing that the dying Trajan had formally adopted Hadrian as son and heir reached Antioch on 9 August 117, two days before the army acclaimed him emperor — a document ancient historians already suspected Trajan's widow Plotina, not Trajan himself, had signed.

properties.name: Trajan abandons the siege of Hatra
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Hatra, Iraq · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Roman legions besieged the desert fortress of Hatra in spring 117 but withdrew after failing to breach its walls, worn down by heat, thirst and disease in a campaign that left the emperor fatally ill for the journey home.

properties.name: Hadrian's accession announced in Alexandria
properties.image_credit: Engraving by Philip Galle, 1572, imagining the Lighthouse of Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 16th-century imagined engraving of the Lighthouse of Alexandria
properties.one_line: Prefect Rammius Martialis's circular letter reached Alexandria's officials on 25 August 117, ordering ten days of garlanded festivals across every Egyptian nome to mark Hadrian's accession — a document that survives as the papyrus P.Oxy. 3781.

properties.name: Senate votes to deify Trajan
properties.image_credit: Curia Julia, Roman Forum, meeting place of the Senate · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Rome's Senate answered Hadrian's accession letter with a unanimous vote deifying Trajan and granting honors beyond what Hadrian had even requested, a reply that reached him in Antioch by late September 117.

properties.name: Unrest breaks out on the British frontier
properties.image_credit: The excavated fort and vicus at Vindolanda, on the northern British frontier · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: The Historia Augusta recorded that 'the Britons could not be kept under Roman control' at the very start of Hadrian's reign in 117 (exact month unrecorded) — the earliest sign of the frontier crisis that led, five years later, to the building of Hadrian's Wall.

properties.name: Roxolani and Iazyges strike the Danube frontier
properties.image_credit: Heidentor triumphal arch at Carnuntum, a fortress on the Danube frontier · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: In autumn 117 the Sarmatian Roxolani and Iazyges struck the Danube frontier provinces of Moesia Inferior and Pannonia, and the fighting cost the governor of Dacia, Quadratus Bassus, his life.

properties.name: Hadrian leaves Antioch for the Danube frontier
properties.image_credit: Roman-era mosaic excavated at Antioch · Wikimedia Commons
properties.one_line: Hadrian left Antioch by the overland route rather than sailing for Rome, driven north by news of the Danube crisis, and had reached Mopsucrene in Cilicia by 13 October 117.
